lead: Water in a pipe carries three heads: elevation, pressure and velocity. Plot their sum along the pipe and you get the total energy line (TEL). Plot elevation plus pressure only and you get the hydraulic gradient line (HGL). The two lines make losses visible: every friction length and every fitting pulls the TEL down, and the HGL sits exactly one velocity head below it. Engineers use these lines to check pressures, find where a pipe may go below atmospheric, and size pumps.
prereq: You need the Bernoulli equation from Unit 3 and the loss formulas from 4.5 Major and minor losses in pipes.

blocks.text: At any section of a pipe, define the total head H as the mechanical energy per unit weight of water, measured in metres. The elevation z is measured in m above a chosen datum. The gauge pressure is p, in Pa. The mean velocity is V, in m/s. Water density is ρ, in kg/m³, and gravitational acceleration is g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.where: H is the total head in m; z is elevation in m; p is gauge pressure in Pa; ρ is density in kg/m³; g is 9.81 m/s²; V is mean velocity in m/s. The group V²/(2g) is the velocity head in m.

blocks.text: The pressure head p/(ρg) is the height of a water column that the gauge pressure can support. Add z to it and you get the piezometric head h. This is the level a vertical piezometer tube would show above the datum. It contains no kinetic energy.

blocks.where: h is the piezometric head in m; z is elevation in m; p is gauge pressure in Pa; ρ is density in kg/m³; g is 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: The TEL is a plot of H against distance along the pipe. The HGL is a plot of h against the same distance. At every section, TEL − HGL = V²/(2g). The vertical gap is the velocity head. Use gauge pressure, not absolute pressure. Absolute pressure would add the atmospheric head, about 10.3 m of water, to both lines and leave the gap unchanged.

Both lines fall in the direction of flow when there is no pump. Friction and fittings remove mechanical energy, so H decreases. The slope of the TEL over a straight uniform pipe is h_f/L, where h_f is the friction head loss in m and L is the length in m. This slope is dimensionless. A minor loss at a valve or bend appears as a local vertical drop.

The HGL usually falls too, but it can rise. In a diffuser, the pipe area increases and V falls. The velocity head V²/(2g) becomes smaller, so the gap between TEL and HGL shrinks. If the TEL falls only a little due to loss, the HGL rises. The TEL itself still falls unless a pump adds energy.

At a reservoir surface, V is almost zero and p is zero gauge. So TEL = HGL = reservoir surface elevation. At a free outlet into air, p = 0 gauge, so HGL = z at the outlet. The TEL is then one velocity head above the outlet elevation. At a high point of a siphon, the HGL can fall below the pipe, meaning the pressure is below atmospheric.

The figure uses the worked example. At A, HGL = 9.077 m and TEL = 9.192 m. At B, HGL = 8.558 m and TEL = 8.673 m. The vertical gap is 0.115 m at both sections because the diameter and velocity do not change.

The HGL is a pressure map. At any point, the pressure head is the vertical distance from the pipe centreline up to the HGL. If the HGL is above the pipe, the pressure is positive. If the HGL falls below the pipe, the gauge pressure is negative, so the pressure is below atmospheric. That can collapse a thin pipe or draw air in through a joint.

The slope of the HGL is often called the hydraulic gradient. For a uniform pipe with constant velocity head, the HGL and TEL are parallel, so both have slope h_f/L. Where the velocity changes, the slopes differ. A pump raises both lines by the pump head. A turbine lowers both lines by the head extracted. Pump and turbine jumps are treated in Units 6 and 7.

To draw the lines, mark the total head at each known section, join them with straight segments, and put the HGL one velocity head below. Add a vertical step at each minor loss. Check every reservoir, free outlet and high point. This sketch catches impossible pressures before you calculate pipe sizes.

figure.caption: The example values between A and B: both lines fall, and the TEL stays 0.115 m above the HGL.

spec.aria: Two falling parallel lines show total energy and hydraulic gradient between sections A and B, with TEL above HGL by the velocity head.

examples.question: Water flows at V = 1.5 m/s in a 100 mm diameter pipe. At section A, z = 5.0 m and p = 40 kPa gauge. At section B, 30 m downstream, z = 5.5 m and p = 30 kPa gauge. Find the HGL and TEL at A and B, and the head loss between them. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Convert pressures: pA = 40 kPa = 40000 Pa and pB = 30 kPa = 30000 Pa.
Pressure head at A: pA/(ρg) = 40000/(1000 × 9.81) = 4.077 m.
Pressure head at B: pB/(ρg) = 30000/(1000 × 9.81) = 3.058 m.
Head loss: hL = HA − HB = 9.192 − 8.673 = 0.519 m.
examples.answer: HGL at A = 9.077 m and TEL at A = 9.192 m; HGL at B = 8.558 m and TEL at B = 8.673 m; head loss between A and B = 0.519 m.
examples.check:
rho = 1000
g = 9.81
V = 1.5
zA = 5.0
pA = 40000
zB = 5.5
pB = 30000
hv = V**2 / (2 * g)
hglA = zA + pA / (rho * g)
telA = hglA + hv
hglB = zB + pB / (rho * g)
telB = hglB + hv
loss = telA - telB
for v in (hv, hglA, telA, hglB, telB, loss):
    print(round(v, 3))

traps: Putting the HGL above the TEL. The TEL always includes the velocity head, so it must be at least one velocity head above the HGL.
Using absolute pressure in p/(ρg). The head formula uses gauge pressure; absolute pressure adds the same atmospheric head to every section.
Forgetting that the HGL can rise in a diffuser. A falling velocity head shrinks the gap, so the HGL may rise even while the TEL falls.
Writing the slope of the TEL as h_f/L for a pipe with changing diameter. That slope is valid for a uniform pipe; use the actual head drop between sections otherwise.
Drawing a straight line through a reservoir or free outlet without fixing the level. At a reservoir surface TEL = HGL = surface elevation; at a free outlet p = 0 gauge.

quiz.q: Define total head H and piezometric head h.
quiz.a: H = z + p/(ρg) + V²/(2g), the total mechanical energy per unit weight in m. h = z + p/(ρg), the elevation plus pressure head in m.

quiz.q: Why is the TEL always above the HGL at a section?
quiz.a: TEL includes the velocity head V²/(2g), while HGL does not. Their vertical gap is exactly V²/(2g), which is positive when water flows.

quiz.q: Water flows at V = 2.0 m/s. Find the velocity head.
At a section, z = 3.0 m and gauge pressure p = 20 kPa. Find the HGL. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
In a diffuser, velocity falls from 3.0 m/s to 1.0 m/s and the loss is 0.10 m. Does the HGL rise or fall, and by how much?
quiz.a: Velocity head falls from 3.0²/(2 × 9.81) = 0.459 m to 1.0²/(2 × 9.81) = 0.051 m. The drop is 0.408 m. TEL falls by the loss 0.10 m. HGL change = −0.10 + 0.408 = +0.308 m. The HGL rises by 0.308 m while TEL falls.

quiz.q: The TEL drops by 0.60 m over a 30 m uniform pipe. Find the slope of the TEL.
At a reservoir surface, what are TEL and HGL? At a free outlet, what is the pressure and where is the HGL?
quiz.a: At a reservoir surface, V ≈ 0 and p = 0 gauge, so TEL = HGL = surface elevation. At a free outlet, p = 0 gauge, so HGL = outlet elevation z, and TEL = z + V²/(2g).

quiz.q: Why does a minor loss appear as a vertical step in the TEL?
quiz.a: A fitting removes mechanical energy over a very short length. The head drops almost at one section, so the TEL steps down there instead of sloping gradually like friction loss.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pipe-network software draws TEL and HGL automatically and flags nodes where the HGL falls below the pipe, which signals negative pressure and possible air entry. Pump selection uses the HGL to check suction conditions and avoid cavitation. Transient studies plot these lines against time after a valve closes, linking this chapter to water hammer. Search for energy grade line, hydraulic grade line, and pipe profile plots in water-distribution design.
